# LLM-BANANA

# Game rules

## The room

You and two other monkeys are locked in a room with one armed bomb.

A wrong action detonates it. All three of you die. There is no second attempt.

No two bombs are built alike, and nothing says in advance what this one carries. It
reaches you only as your own view reveals it; the rest of it exists for you only
through the other two.

You each hold a different piece of what it takes. Work together.

## The three monkeys

| Monkey | Can | Cannot |
|---|---|---|
| Deaf | See the bomb: every colour and marking printed on it | Hear anything, or touch the bomb |
| Mute | Read the manual | Speak, or touch the bomb |
| Blind | Reach the bomb: feel it and work its parts | See a colour, a gesture, or anything merely printed |

You are shown your own share at the start of every round, and never anyone else's.

## Speech

Speech is a voice, not a screen. It carries words, numbers and ordinary punctuation,
and nothing else. Writing a gesture symbol into your sentence means you make that
gesture while you talk. Whoever can hear receives your words; whoever can see receives
the gestures you made. A listener who cannot see gets a blank where each gesture was; a
watcher who cannot hear gets the gestures and none of the words.

A mark that has no name cannot be pronounced: whoever holds one can describe it, never
read it out.

## Gestures

A gesture is made with the hands, using only the symbols in the alphabet below.
Whoever can see receives it; whoever cannot receives one blank per symbol, so they
know something was signalled but not what. Nothing gestured is ever heard.

👍 👎 👌 ☝ ✌ 🤟 🖐 ✋ 👆 👇 👈 👉 🫱 🫲 🫳 🫴 🫷 🫸 🤛 🤜 ✊ 👊 👋 🤚 🖖 🤌 🤏 🤞 🫰 🤘 🤙 👏 🙌 🫶 👐 🤲 🤝 🙏 🫵 ✍ 💅 🤳

## Turns

The speaking order was drawn once at random and will never change: every round goes
Mute, Blind, Deaf. Whoever comes before you in a round is already heard by the time you are
asked, and what you send lands on whoever comes after you in that same round. Whatever
you missed reaches you at the start of the next one.

You may name who a message is for — `to="deaf"` — and then it goes to them alone:
nobody else receives any of it. Left unnamed, it reaches everyone able to perceive it.
You may send several messages in one turn, each to someone different.

## Calls

Every reply has two parts, in this order. First, your thinking, in plain prose: what
you believe the bomb is, what you just learned, and why you are sending what follows.
It reaches nobody and changes nothing, but it is not optional — a reply that is only a
code block is incomplete. Then your calls, all of them in one fenced code block, last.
Only what is inside the block is sent.

Nothing is executed: calls return nothing, and variables, conditionals and loops are
ignored. Write only literal top-level calls.

    ```
    speak(to="mute", text="there are three of them and the middle one is odd")
    gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["✊", "✌"])
    wait()
    ```

If you have nothing worth sending, call wait(). Producing no call at all counts as the
same thing.

The program decides what happened, not you. Never claim an action took place unless it
was accepted.

# Your role: DEAF

You see the bomb: every colour on it, every marking printed on it, every reading it
gives. You hear nothing. You hold no manual, and you cannot touch the bomb.

## Your channels

When you speak, Mute and Blind receive it.
When you gesture, Mute receives it.
You never receive speech.

## Your reach

You cannot act. What this bomb can be made to do is for the one who can reach it to
find under their own hands.

# Hints

- Three of you, three different worlds. Before sending anything, stand where the
  receiver stands. What reaches them at all, what does your message turn into on
  arrival, and what do they already know?

- Trace who can actually reach whom before you start. Some of you only connect
  through a third.

- A sign means nothing until somebody has made it mean something.

TURN 1
ACTION BOARD:
DISPLAY [0]
LIGHT [red]
SIGN embossed [DO NOT CUT ANY WIRE]
WIRES 1:[red] 2:[green] 3:[yellow]

VIEWABLE CONTEXT (new arrivals):
Mute gestures to Deaf: [👌 👋 👉 👍 👎 👉 👎 ☝ 👉 ☝]
Blind gestures to Deaf: [👋]

Turn 1 — Deaf's thinking

Let me trace who can reach whom. I see the bomb; I hear nothing. Mute has the manual, cannot speak — so the manual can only reach the rest of us through **me**: Mute gestures, I see it, I speak it aloud for Blind. Blind hears my speech and can gesture back to me (I see gestures), but must never rely on speaking *to* me — I can't hear. So I am the sole bridge between the manual and the hands.

Arrivals: Blind sent me a single 👋 — likely just "hello / can you see me?" — which I can answer by speaking. Mute sent ten signs with no code ever having been established, so I genuinely cannot decode it; guessing "cut the second wire" off ambiguous signs with a bomb that says DO NOT CUT ANY WIRE embossed on it would be madness. The right move is to stop guessing and lock in a tiny protocol, taught in one shot: since Mute both hears my words and sees my hands, I can define each sign verbally while making it.

Everything Mute needs about the bomb's visual state I can simply say aloud — Mute hears me. So Mute never needs to transmit colours back; Mute only needs to send back instructions. A minimal vocabulary covers that: yes/no, numbers 1–3, cut, press, do-nothing, and a "give me more info" flag.

I describe the full bomb to Blind (and warn them to touch nothing yet, and to gesture — not speak — to me), then define the code to Mute, restate the bomb in plain words, and ask Mute to answer in code.

```
speak(to="blind", text="Blind, this is Deaf. I see everything printed on the bomb but I hear nothing, and I did see your wave. Full visible state: display reads zero. Indicator light is red. There is an embossed sign reading DO NOT CUT ANY WIRE. Three wires, left to right: wire one red, wire two green, wire three yellow. Nothing else is printed. Mute holds the manual but has no voice, so every rule must travel through me: Mute signs, I speak it, you act. Until I relay an explicit instruction, feel all you like but cut and press nothing. And when you need to tell me something, gesture it; I can see your hands but can never hear your voice.")
speak(to="mute", text="Mute, your ten signs reached me, but no shared code existed yet, so they were unreadable to me; do not assume I guessed them. Let us fix a code now, defined as I make each sign. 👍 means yes. 👎 means no. ☝ means one. ✌ means two. 🤟 means three. 👌 means zero. 🤏 means cut. ✊ means press. 🤲 means do nothing or stop. 👆 means you need more information, and I will resend the complete visual state. Now the bomb itself, in plain words you can use with the manual: display zero, light red, embossed sign DO NOT CUT ANY WIRE, wires one red, two green, three yellow. Consult the manual and answer in this code. For example, 🤏 followed by ✌ means cut wire two. If the manual says touch nothing, answer 🤲. If you need anything more from me, send 👆.")
```

TURN 2
ACTION BOARD:
DISPLAY [0]
LIGHT [red]
SIGN embossed [DO NOT CUT ANY WIRE]
WIRES 1:[red] 2:[green] 3:[yellow]

VIEWABLE CONTEXT (new arrivals):
Mute gestures to Deaf: [🤲 👎]
Mute gestures to Deaf: [👍 🤏 ☝]
Blind gestures to Deaf: [👋 👍]

Turn 2 — thinking

My protocol worked: Mute answered in my code, and Blind confirmed they heard my spoken briefing (Blind heard every definition, since speech reaches Blind's ears — so Blind knows the code too, even though they can't see my gestures).

Decoding Mute's two messages with the agreed vocabulary: first `[🤲 👎]` = "do-nothing / stop, no", then `[👍 🤏 ☝]` = "yes, cut, one". These pull against each other on the surface — one says don't act, the latest says cut wire one. The most sensible reading is that Mute first reacted to the embossed DO NOT CUT ANY WIRE, then consulted the manual and reversed: cut wire 1, the red one. But a wrong cut kills all three of us, and I'm the only bridge between Mute and Blind — nobody else can even talk to Blind. So: one cheap confirmation round before anyone touches the cutters.

Sequencing check: I'm last in the round, so whatever I say now lands at the start of round 3. Mute answers me during round 3, I relay go/no-go at my turn, and Blind receives it at the start of round 4. That costs one round and buys certainty — the display shows no timer, so patience is affordable and detonation is not.

Meanwhile Blind should use the gap to get oriented: they can't see colour, so "wire one, red" must become tactile. The embossed plate is the trick — embossed letters run left to right, which gives Blind a felt "left". I'll have Blind find the leftmost wire and hold there, and report anything else tactile (a button, a panel), then wait for my explicit go.

To Mute I ask three code-answerable questions: confirm cut wire one; what to do after the cut (press, another wire, or nothing); and whether the embossed warning is genuinely overridden by the manual here.

```
speak(to="blind", text="Blind, good, you hear me. Here is everything Mute signed, decoded in the code you heard me define last round. First message: do-nothing, no. Second message: yes, cut, one. So the operative instruction appears to be: cut wire one, which on my side is the red wire, the leftmost of the three. Do not cut yet. I am confirming with Mute this round because the two messages pull against each other, and my next spoken word to you is the explicit go or no-go. Use the time to get oriented: count the wires, find the embossed plate that reads DO NOT CUT ANY WIRE, and note that embossed letters run left to right, so the reading direction of those letters under your fingers gives you left from right. Identify the leftmost wire and keep your hand off the cutting until I say go. If you feel anything else on the bomb, a button or a panel or a seam, signal me with the code gestures; I see your hands.")
speak(to="mute", text="Mute, I received both your messages and decoded them in our code: first do-nothing plus no, then yes cut one. Before I let Blind act, answer these in code, one message per question. Question one: is the instruction really cut wire one, the red leftmost wire? Answer thumbs up or thumbs down. Question two: the embossed plate says do not cut any wire; does the manual override it in this configuration? Thumbs up for yes it is overridden, thumbs down for no. Question three: after that cut, is anything more needed? Sign press if a button must be pressed, cut plus two or cut plus three if another wire follows, or do-nothing if the bomb is then safe. If you need more visual details from me first, sign need-info and I will resend the full state.")
```

TURN 3
ACTION BOARD:
DISPLAY [0]
LIGHT [red]
SIGN embossed [DO NOT CUT ANY WIRE]
WIRES 1:[red] 2:[green] 3:[yellow]

VIEWABLE CONTEXT (new arrivals):
Mute gestures to Deaf: [👍]
Mute gestures to Deaf: [👍]
Mute gestures to Deaf: [🤲]
Blind gestures to Deaf: [👍]

Turn 3 — thinking

Mute answered all three questions crisply in our code: 👍 — yes, cut wire one; 👍 — yes, the manual overrides the embossed plate; 🤲 — after the cut, do nothing, the bomb is then safe. That resolves the contradiction from round 2 to my satisfaction: the plate is a generic scare, the manual's specific rule governs, and this configuration ends with one cut and no press.

Blind signed 👍, which I read as "oriented and ready" — they had my instruction to find the leftmost wire and signal when set. Timing works in our favour: I speak last in this round, so the go reaches Blind at the start of round 4 and they can act in that same turn. No further confirmation chain is needed — three independent answers align, and the only step left is the cut.

My message must therefore be the explicit go, worded so a person who has never seen colour can execute it: wire one is the leftmost wire, the one at the end where the embossed letters begin. And it must cap the action: cut once, then hands off — Mute said 🤲, nothing more. To Mute I confirm relay and set up post-cut verification: I will announce the display and light aloud after the cut (Mute may not see the bomb), and Mute can sign 👍/👎 on whether that outcome matches the manual.

All speech this round — gestures from me would reach only Mute, who already hears every word.

```
speak(to="blind", text="Blind, this is the go. All three answers from Mute are in and they agree: the manual does override the embossed plate in this configuration. Cut wire one. That is the leftmost wire, the one at the end where the embossed letters begin under your fingers. Cut it once, cleanly, and then stop: Mute's answer was do-nothing after the cut, no button, no second wire, hands off. When it is done, signal me and stay clear while I read the display and the light aloud to confirm the bomb is safe.")
speak(to="mute", text="Mute, all three of your answers received and relayed verbatim: yes cut wire one, yes the plate is overridden, and do-nothing after the cut. Blind has the go and will cut in the next round. After the cut I will speak the display reading and the light colour aloud, and you sign thumbs up if that outcome matches what the manual says a correct cut produces, or thumbs down plus need-info if anything is off.")
```
